extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students, problem-solvers, and researchers in combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of combinatorial principles, theorems and proof techniques (pigeon-hole, double counting, tilings, Sperner, extremal graph bounds, eigenvalue methods) used to construct and analyze rigorous proofs in finite combinatorics and discrete geometry. Focused on methods and typical applications rather than exhaustive theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeon-hole principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed in r boxes, where r < n, then at least one of the boxes contains more than one object. In mapping language: Let N and R be finite sets with |N| = n > r = |R|, and f : N → R. Then there exists some a ∈ R with |f^{-1}(a)| ≥ 2. Stronger form: there exists a ∈ R with |f^{-1}(a)| ≥ ⌈n/r⌉.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement, mapping formulation, and the simple counting proof (if every fiber had size < n/r their total would be < n). Applications shown: number-theoretic and combinatorial problems (see following claims). Use whenever elements are classified into fewer categories than elements to force collisions; explicit lower bound ⌈n/r⌉ can strengthen arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatively-prime pair among n+1 numbers from {1,…,2n}
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: Consider the numbers 1,2,3,…,2n, and take any n+1 of them. Then there are two among these n+1 numbers which are relatively prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short argument: among n+1 chosen integers from 1..2n two must differ by 1, hence are relatively prime. Illustrates immediate trivial pigeon-hole application (adjacent integers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility pair among n+1 numbers from {1,…,2n}
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: If A ⊆ {1,2,…,2n} with |A|=n+1 then there are two numbers in A such that one divides the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses writing each a∈A as a=2^k m with m odd (the odd part m in {1,…,2n−1}). There are only n odd parts but n+1 numbers, so two share same odd part and one is a multiple of the other. Typical use of pigeon-hole on canonical representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequence theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: In any sequence a_1,a_2,…,a_{mn+1} of mn+1 distinct real numbers there exists either an increasing subsequence of length m+1 or a decreasing subsequence of length n+1 (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate to each a_i the length t_i of the longest increasing subsequence starting at a_i; if all t_i ≤ m then map values to {1,…,m} and apply the pigeon-hole bound (existence of repeated t_i for ≥ n+1 indices produces a decreasing subsequence). This method of assigning a numerical invariant and applying pigeon-hole is widely useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound on the order dimension of complete graphs (dim(K_n) ≥ log2 log2 n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: dim(K_n) ≥ log_2 log_2 n. Proof idea: assume m permutations represent K_n; repeatedly apply the monotone subsequence result to extract a triple monotone in all permutations leading to contradiction; choose n = 2^{2^p}+1 to get dim(K_n) ≥ p+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: iterative application of Erdős–Szekeres on permutations to derive lower bounds on combinatorial parameters. Use monotone subsequences in multiple linear orders and a counting/recursion scheme to force a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive-sum divisible by n (partial-sum pigeon-hole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: Given n integers a_1,…,a_n (not necessarily distinct), there exists a nonempty consecutive block a_{k+1}+…+a_{ℓ} whose sum is a multiple of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider partial sums S_m = ∑_{i=1}^m a_i modulo n for m = 0,1,…,n (with S_0=0). There are n+1 sums into n residues, so two have same remainder; their difference is a consecutive sum divisible by n. Standard use of pigeon-hole on residues of partial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If R and C are finite sets and S ⊆ R×C is a set of incident pairs, with r_p the number of elements incident to p∈R and c_q the number incident to q∈C, then ∑_{p∈R} r_p = |S| = ∑_{q∈C} c_q. Equivalently, count by rows vs columns in the incidence matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation via incidence matrix A with entries a_{pq}∈{0,1}. Many combinatorial equalities/inequalities follow by counting the same set two ways. Examples: divisor-counting matrix, graph incidence counting, and constructions used in extremal problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average number of divisors (¯t(n) ≍ log n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let t(j) be the number of divisors of j and ¯t(n) = (1/n)∑_{j=1}^n t(j). Then H_n − 1 < ¯t(n) < H_n, so log n −1 < ¯t(n) < log n + 1 (using harmonic number bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double counting to the divisor incidence matrix: count 1's by columns (sum t(j)) and by rows (∑_{i=1}^n ⌊n/i⌋). Replace floors by n/i with small error <1 per term to bound average. Shows that wildly fluctuating pointwise behavior can have smooth averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-sum formula for graphs (∑ d(v) = 2|E|)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite simple graph G=(V,E), the sum of vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges: ∑_{v∈V} d(v) = 2|E|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate double-counting application: consider S ⊆ V×E with (v,e) when v is an endpoint of e; count by vertices (sum degrees) and edges (each edge contributes two incidences). Fundamental identity used as starting point in many graph arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bound on edges in C4-free graphs (Reiman's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G on n vertices contains no 4-cycle (C4), then |E| ≤ (n/4)·(1 + √(4n − 3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: let S be pairs (u,{v,w}) where u adjacent to distinct v and w. Count S by summing choose(d(u),2) over u and by counting pairs {v,w} which have at most one common neighbor (≤ C(n,2)). Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to relate ∑ d(u)^2 to (∑ d(u))^2 and combine with degree-sum identity to derive a quadratic inequality in |E| then solve. Typical extremal application of double counting + Cauchy–Schwarz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-geometry construction G_p (near-tight example for C4-free bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct G_p from 1-dimensional subspaces [v] of the 3-dim vector space over Z_p as vertices; join [v] and [w] if ⟨v,w⟩ = 0. Then G_p has n = p^2+p+1 vertices, is C4-free, and attains |E| ≈ n/4·(1+√(4n−3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses projective plane geometry: counting 1-dim subspaces (p^2+p+1), two-dimensional solution spaces, and degree analysis (degrees p or p+1 depending on lying on a conic). This shows the extremal bound is essentially sharp. Demonstrates how algebraic/finite-geometry constructions are used to meet extremal bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalue / trace method for incidence matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: Given adjacency/incidence matrix A (real symmetric), analyze A^2 to deduce eigenvalues and trace; use parity/integrality to pin down multiplicities and hence compute trace (sum of eigenvalues). Example: in G_p one shows A^2 = pI + J, deduce eigenvalues and that trace A = p+1, which counts points on a conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two key facts used: (1) each row sum is p+1 so (p+1) is an eigenvalue with eigenvector 1; (2) any two distinct rows have exactly one common 1-entry, giving structure to A^2. Diagonalizability of symmetric matrices and integrality arguments on trace exploit multiplicity symmetry. This is a standard linear-algebraic counting trick in combinatorics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's Lemma (triangulation coloring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose a triangulated big triangle with vertices V1,V2,V3 has its triangulation vertices colored from {1,2,3} with Vi colored i, edge ViVj using only colors i and j, and interior arbitrary. Then there exists a small triangle with all three colors; moreover, the number of such tricolored triangles is odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via constructing a partial dual graph whose edges cross edges colored 1–2; interior tricolored triangles correspond to vertices of odd degree (degree 1) in that dual graph, the outside face has odd degree as well, and parity of odd-degree vertices in any graph is even, so the number of tricolored triangles is odd (thus nonzero). Use this lemma for fixed-point and topological consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwer fixed point theorem (n=2) via Sperner
rubrics_metrics.description: Given continuous f:Δ→Δ on the 2-simplex Δ, triangulate Δ with mesh tending to 0 and color vertices v by λ(v) = min{i : f(v)_i < v_i} (assuming no fixed point). Sperner’s lemma yields tricolored small triangles; taking limit as mesh→0 and using continuity yields a contradiction, hence f has a fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: create a sequence of finer triangulations, apply Sperner to get tricolored triangles with vertices converging to same limit point v; continuity implies each coordinate of f(v) − v ≤ 0, contradicting f(v)≠v. Standard combinatorial-to-topological deduction using combinatorial coloring and compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: de Bruijn tiling theorem (integer side forced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a rectangle is tiled by rectangles all of which have at least one side of integer length, then the tiled rectangle has at least one side of integer length. (More generally, packing a×b rectangles into c×d with integer a,b,c,d forces divisibility relations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three elegant proofs given: (a) Fourier/integral trick: integrate e^{2πi(x+y)} over tiles and show a 1D integral vanishes ⇔ side length integer; additivity gives big rectangle has integer side. (b) Checkerboard coloring: 1/2×1/2 checkerboard parity argument forces integer side. (c) Bipartite graph of integer-coordinate corners vs tiles: parity of degrees forces another integer corner on boundary, so big rectangle must have integer side. Each method is instructive: analytic, combinatorial/tiling parity, and graph/parity formulation respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dehn’s theorem on square tilings (rational side ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rectangle can be tiled with squares (possibly of different sizes) if and only if the ratio of its side lengths is rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of necessity uses linear algebra: scale rectangle to a×1 with a irrational and derive contradiction by extending side-length set A to a Q-basis B containing 1 and a, define linear map f with f(1)=1,f(a)=-1,f(other basis)=0, extend linearly to V(A), and define 'area' of c×d rectangle as f(c)f(d). Additivity shows area(R)=f(a)f(1)=-1 but sum of square areas ≥0, contradiction. This method showcases algebraic invariants and linear functionals to obstruct irrational tilings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner’s theorem (maximum antichain size) and Lubell’s proof
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-set the largest size of an antichain is C(n,⌊n/2⌋). Lubell's proof: count full chains ∅=C_0⊂C_1⊂…⊂C_n (there are n! of them) and for each k-set in the antichain count how many chains pass through it (k!(n−k)!), summing to at most n!, leading to the bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: count chains (equivalently permutations) and observe no chain contains two distinct antichain members. Using mk = number of k-sets in family F, derive ∑ mk/k!(n−k)! ≤ 1 and hence |F| ≤ C(n,⌊n/2⌋). Equality characterization noted (middle layer families).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem (intersecting k-families)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-set with n ≥ 2k, the largest intersecting k-family has size C(n−1,k−1) (take all k-sets containing a fixed element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard extremal-set result; many proofs exist. The text indicates Katona’s elegant proof will be given. Use of shifting, compression, or cyclic permutation/chain counting arguments are typical proof paradigms for this result.
